items.name: Status Board
items.summary: Poll a list of internal endpoints and show what is up, slow or down.
items.description: A status page for the services your team runs. It polls each endpoint from inside the network on an interval and shows the result as a board, with the last error text when there is one. Go, standard library only — no database, no external assets, nothing persisted: the board is what the process has seen since it started.
items.author: Launchpad

env.name: SERVICES
env.description: Comma-separated name=url pairs, e.g. Wiki=https://wiki.internal/health, Billing=https://billing.internal/healthz

env.name: BOARD_TITLE
env.description: Heading shown on the page.

env.name: CHECK_INTERVAL_SECONDS
env.description: How often every endpoint is polled. Minimum 5.

env.name: CHECK_TIMEOUT_SECONDS
env.description: Per-request timeout. Minimum 1.

items.notes: The board makes outbound HTTP requests to whatever SERVICES names. Point it only at endpoints this install is meant to reach.

items.name: Webhook Inspector
items.summary: See exactly what a third party is sending you: method, headers, query and body.
items.description: Point any webhook at this app's /hook path and every request is captured and shown newest first. FastAPI. Nothing is persisted — the buffer lives in the process and is lost on restart, which is the right trade for a tool that routinely receives signatures, customer identifiers and one-time tokens. Authorization, Cookie and X-API-Key are recorded as redacted rather than dropped, because 'did they send one at all' is usually the real question.
items.author: Launchpad

env.name: MAX_REQUESTS
env.description: How many requests to keep in memory. 1 to 500.

env.name: WEBHOOK_TOKEN
env.description: Optional shared secret. When set, a capture must carry X-Webhook-Token or ?token=.

items.notes: The token is a convenience for handing the URL to an external sender, not a boundary — the app already sits behind Launchpad's authorization.

items.name: Ops Console
items.summary: On-call, the operations checklist by cadence, and four short runbooks.
items.description: An internal operations console for the team that runs the platform. Next.js App Router, React 19, no dependencies beyond the framework. It reads no platform API at all: checklists and runbooks are content in the repository, and only what genuinely differs per install — team name, who is on call — comes from the environment.
items.author: Launchpad

env.name: TEAM_NAME
env.description: Heading on the overview.

env.name: ONCALL_PRIMARY
env.description: Who is holding the pager.

env.name: ONCALL_SECONDARY
env.description: Who takes the weekly work.

env.name: ESCALATION_CHANNEL
env.description: Where to escalate when the primary is unreachable.

items.notes: The overview is rendered per request, so changing an on-call name and restarting the app is enough — no rebuild.

items.name: Flask Hello
items.summary: The smallest complete Flask app — and the four things one has to get right here.
items.description: A hello page that demonstrates a module-level app the Flask CLI can find, ProxyFix with x_prefix so url_for() emits links under /apps/{slug}, configuration from the environment, and a health endpoint that reports something real. The page shows the forwarded headers live, so removing the ProxyFix line and watching the links break is a two-minute lesson.
items.author: Launchpad

env.name: GREETING
env.description: The heading, and the greeting the JSON endpoint returns.

items.notes: An example arrives as an ordinary uploaded app: it is yours to edit, and it is never updated from the catalog.

items.name: CSV Explorer
items.summary: Upload a CSV, filter it, chart it, and take the cleaned data away again.
items.description: A Streamlit app that is useful the day it is deployed. It ships with a seeded sample dataset so there is something on screen before anybody uploads anything, and uploaded data is held in session state and never written to disk — on a shared install a file written into the app's directory is one every other viewer can read.
items.author: Launchpad

env.name: APP_TITLE
env.description: Page title and heading.

items.notes: Streamlit is the one framework that keeps the /apps/{slug} prefix rather than having it stripped; the platform passes it with --server.baseUrlPath.

items.name: Next.js Dashboard
items.summary: Stat tiles, a range switcher and a line chart — with no chart library.
items.description: A metrics dashboard on the App Router: server components throughout except one client island for the chart, which is eighty lines of SVG rather than a 300 kB dependency. The selected metric and range live in the URL, so a view is a link somebody can paste into a chat. The data is generated from a seed in lib/metrics.js — swap that file for a query and nothing else changes.
items.author: Launchpad
items.notes: Do not set basePath or NODE_ENV on a Next.js app here: Launchpad injects the first at build time, and the second makes npm drop the devDependencies the build needs.

items.name: Node API
items.summary: A REST API and the page that uses it, on Express — the generic Node path.
items.description: A task list with GET, POST, PATCH and DELETE, and a UI that calls it. The example is really about the three things that separate 'works locally' from 'works on the platform': binding HOST rather than 0.0.0.0, listening on PORT, and building client-side URLs relative to the document instead of the root.
items.author: Launchpad
items.notes: Any package.json with a start script is hostable this way; the app is told its mount point through BASE_PATH and the proxy strips the prefix.

items.name: Weekly Report
items.summary: A working web app that is only the Python standard library.
items.description: A weekly delivery report rendered by http.server, with the same numbers offered as JSON and CSV. Because nothing supplies a server, the app owns the whole platform contract: it listens on PORT, binds HOST, uses BASE_PATH only for URLs that leave the process, and handles SIGTERM so a deploy does not kill it mid-response. Replace data.py with a query and app.py is unchanged.
items.author: Launchpad

env.name: REPORT_TITLE
env.description: Heading and page title.

items.notes: This is the generic Python path: a requirements.txt naming none of the recognised frameworks means the app is started as `python app.py`.

items.name: MCP Server
items.summary: A Model Context Protocol server an assistant can connect to — hosted like any other app.
items.description: MCP's streamable-HTTP transport is an HTTP server, so a remote MCP server is an ordinary Launchpad app and this one is 250 lines of Python. It serves three tools over a folder of Markdown runbooks — list, search, read — and the notes it ships are samples to delete. What is worth copying is the shape: no authentication inside the app, because the gateway already refuses anything without an API key and strips the credential before it arrives; stateless sessions, so a deploy or an idle sleep can replace the process underneath a connected client; a landing page that works out its own endpoint URL from the forwarded headers; and every path a caller supplies resolved and checked to be inside the folder.
items.author: Launchpad

env.name: SERVER_NAME
env.description: What the server calls itself to a client, and the heading on its endpoint page.

env.name: NOTES_DIR
env.description: The folder of Markdown the tools read. Relative paths are resolved inside the app's directory.

items.notes: The app has no authentication of its own: create a key on its Settings → API keys tab and give it to the client as a bearer token. A client that can send a static Authorization header connects; one that requires MCP's OAuth flow cannot, because Launchpad authenticates with keys and runs no authorization server. The MCP SDK needs Python 3.10+, which the bundled .python-version asks uv to fetch at build time.

items.name: Stockroom
items.summary: An inventory register that gets its own report out: PDF, Slack, email, on demand or on a schedule.
items.description: Five aisles, forty lines, and every receipt and issue on a ledger written in the same transaction as the count it changes. Go with the standard library and html/template; SQLite embedded through modernc.org/sqlite, because Launchpad builds Go apps with CGO off. One report is built once and rendered three ways, so the PDF, the Slack comment and the email body cannot quote different numbers. This is the example to read for an app talking back to Launchpad without an SDK: /api/v1/app/self, the two notify routes, the run list and a scheduled task's own log, spoken directly in about two hundred lines.
items.author: Launchpad

env.name: APP_NAME
env.description: The wordmark, the PDF header, and the name this app's mail is sent under.

env.name: STOCKROOM_DATA_DIR
env.description: Where the SQLite file goes. Leave it unset: the app prefers a writable storage mount, then the scratch directory, and says on its Platform tab which one it picked.

items.notes: Slack and email are absent until an administrator attaches them on the app's Integrations tab, and the app says so rather than offering a button that cannot work. On a shared-mode install the register lives on scratch, so a redeploy re-seeds it — which is the point of the example, not a limitation of it.

items.name: Service Catalog
items.summary: A directory of what runs, who owns it, and what calls what — one page and one JSON file.
items.description: The static hosting example: HTML, CSS, one JavaScript file and data/services.json, with nothing built and nothing installed. Twenty-four invented services across seven teams, searchable by name, tag, team, language or on-call rotation, sortable by tier or by how many other services depend on one. Selecting a service draws its wiring — what it calls on the left, what calls it on the right — both read off the same depends_on array, so the two halves cannot disagree. Read it for the rule that catches everyone: the app is served under /apps/{slug}/, so every URL here is relative, and a root-absolute one would ask Launchpad for a file it does not have.
items.author: Launchpad
items.notes: No configuration and no environment variables: a static app runs no commands and has no dependencies. Editing the catalog means editing data/services.json and redeploying — the release is the site.

items.name: Volume Browser
items.summary: Browse, upload and manage the EFS volumes attached to an app.
items.description: A file manager for attached storage. It reads LAUNCHPAD_STORAGE — the platform's own declaration of what is mounted — and offers the ordinary operations on every EFS volume it finds: browse, download, upload, new folder, rename and delete. Nothing is configured by hand, and a mount that is declared but not on the filesystem is shown with the reason rather than left out. Object stores are listed and deliberately not browsable: Mountpoint has no rename, no append and no real directories. Go, standard library only. Isolated mode, since durable storage is attached below a boundary a shared process does not have.
items.author: Launchpad

env.name: BROWSER_TITLE
env.description: Heading shown on the page.

env.name: MAX_UPLOAD_MB
env.description: Per-file upload limit in megabytes. A file over it is refused and nothing partial is left behind.

env.name: READ_ONLY
env.description: Set to 1 to show every volume read-only regardless of how it is mounted.

items.notes: Attach the volumes this app should manage, then redeploy it — a storage mapping takes effect on the next deployment. It shows whatever those mounts contain to anyone who can open the app, so keep its visibility to the people who should see the data.

items.name: Orders
items.summary: Read a SQLite database off an attached EFS volume — sortable, filterable, read-only.
items.description: The reading side of the storage example: something else — a nightly export, an operations job, a person with the volume browser — leaves orders.db on an EFS volume, and this app shows the orders table as a list you can sort, filter and download as CSV. Python, standard library only: http.server, sqlite3, csv, html. It finds the volume from LAUNCHPAD_STORAGE (the first declared one, never an object store, because Mountpoint has no file locking and SQLite needs it) and opens the file read-only, so it can never be the process that damages the data it shows. The half worth reading is what happens when the database is not there yet, which on a volume is normal for a while: the page names the volume, the exact path it expected and what has to happen, and a Check again button re-reads the declaration and re-stats the mount — nothing is cached, so the file arriving needs no redeploy. Sorting and filtering arrive on the query string, so the schema is discovered with PRAGMA table_info and a sort column is accepted only if the schema just named it; filter text is always a bound parameter.
items.author: Launchpad

env.name: VIEWER_TITLE
env.description: Heading and page title.

env.name: ORDERS_DB
env.description: The database file, relative to the volume root. A path that would leave the volume is refused.

env.name: ORDERS_TABLE
env.description: The table or view to show. If it is missing, the page lists the tables that are there.

env.name: PAGE_SIZE
env.description: Rows per page. Clamped to 10-1000.

items.notes: Needs isolated mode and an EFS volume attached, because a shared process has no boundary to mount storage below. A storage mapping takes effect on the next deployment, so redeploy after attaching one. The app never writes: the connection is read-only, which also means a database in WAL mode cannot be opened from a read-only mount — ship it with PRAGMA journal_mode=DELETE. tools/make_orders_db.py in the repo writes a sample orders.db to upload.

items.name: Request Desk
items.summary: A request-and-approval desk on embedded SQLite, where who may do what comes from the identity Launchpad supplies.
items.description: Somebody asks for a monitor, a conference ticket, a licence; somebody else approves or refuses it. FastAPI and the standard library's sqlite3 — no JavaScript framework, no build step, nothing beyond the two lines in requirements.txt. What it is really for is the seam underneath: Launchpad answers one question the app cannot forge — who is looking — by resolving the signed act-for blob the request arrives with, and everything after that is the app's own directory, its own groups and its own rule. Three sources of authority, deliberately not one. The platform's role on the app (owner, editor, install administrator) administers the desk and nothing else, because 'may redeploy this app' is not 'may approve an expense'; a desk group an editor put you in is the ordinary path; and a desk group linked to a Launchpad group is the same thing with the directory doing the bookkeeping. Two groups ship — Requesters and Approvers — and both are ordinary rows an editor can reshape. An Access page renders the identity the platform supplied beside the decision the app made and the sentences connecting them, which is the part worth reading before building your own. desk.py imports nothing from Launchpad, so the rule is tested without a running install: 31 tests construct callers by hand.
items.author: Launchpad

env.name: DESK_TITLE
env.description: Heading and page title.

env.name: DB_PATH
env.description: Where the SQLite file lives. Unset, the app uses the first writable volume mapped to it, and failing that its own filesystem — which a restart replaces. The page footer always says which of the three it got.

items.notes: Two things have to be true before it can recognise anybody. Viewer identity must be switched on for this app — it is off by default and a system administrator turns it on — and the app must not be public, because Launchpad withholds the email address from a public app and the address is how this desk identifies people. The app explains both on the page rather than looking broken. For data that survives a restart, map a volume: that means isolated mode, since shared mode refuses a storage mapping at deploy time.

items.name: Support Review
items.summary: A notebook executed once at deploy time and served as the document that fell out.
items.description: The notebook example. One .ipynb at the root of a repository is an app: Launchpad installs its requirements.txt, executes every cell once at deploy time with the app's own environment, and serves the HTML at /apps/{slug}/ — there is no kernel behind the published page, and a wake, a crash restore or a repair serves the same file. The report is a monthly support-desk review — arrival volume by team, first response against a configurable target, and the open backlog by age — drawn from a seeded generator, so replacing one cell with a query is the whole of adopting it. What is worth reading is the framework rather than the data: configuration comes from the environment and is clamped, because a cell that raises fails the deploy and a report should not be taken down by somebody typing 'twelve' into a settings box; and the closing cell prints the variable names it read and deliberately not their values, because whatever a cell prints ends up in the published document and on a public app published means the internet.
items.author: Launchpad

env.name: REVIEW_TITLE
env.description: The line the report opens with.

env.name: TEAMS
env.description: Comma-separated team names. The first eight are used.

env.name: PERIOD_WEEKS
env.description: How many weeks the review covers. Clamped to 4-52.

env.name: SLA_HOURS
env.description: The first-response target in hours. Clamped to 1-168.

items.notes: Nothing is re-rendered by a restart: to refresh the numbers, deploy again, or give the app's Overview tab a re-render schedule, which is a full deploy on a cron expression. The engine is nbconvert, the default for an .ipynb; a repo wanting a contents sidebar, code folding and callouts declares [notebook] engine = "quarto" instead, which is refused rather than substituted on an install whose operator has not installed Quarto. Jobs work here, unlike on a static app — a notebook release has an interpreter — but viewer identity does not, because at run time there is no process to hold an app token.

items.name: A/B Test
items.summary: Two variants' visitors and conversions in, and a difference, a confidence interval and a p-value out.
items.description: The Shiny example. Type in the numbers from two variants and the app runs a two-proportion test — but the verdict line is deliberately not the whole answer: the interval underneath it is what separates 'there is no effect' from 'this test was too small to see one', and a second tab answers the question people actually arrive with, which is how many they need before it is worth looking at. No data files, no database, nothing stored, so the app is the same on every install. What is worth copying is the shape rather than the statistics: nothing binds a port and nothing builds a URL, because Launchpad starts a Shiny app by evaluating shiny::runApp(appDir, host, port) and Shiny derives its own asset and WebSocket paths from the page it is served at; and configuration is read into ordinary variables at the top of app.R rather than inside a reactive, because an environment variable is configuration and changing it is a restart.
items.author: Launchpad

env.name: APP_TITLE
env.description: Page title and heading.

env.name: SIGNIFICANCE_LEVEL
env.description: The threshold, as a proportion. Anything outside 0 to 0.5 falls back to 0.05.

items.notes: One R process serves everybody: Shiny is single-threaded, so a reactive that takes four seconds is a four-second queue for every viewer at once, not just the one who moved the slider. That is why everything here is prop.test and power.prop.test rather than a simulation. Anything genuinely slow belongs in a Launchpad job the page polls for, never in a reactive.

items.name: Stats API
items.summary: R's base statistics behind five HTTP routes, for a service that would rather not reimplement them.
items.description: The plumber example. Five routes — a summary with Tukey's fences, a least-squares trend with prediction intervals, Welch's t-test and Mann-Whitney side by side, a PNG histogram, and a health check that names the R version — all computed from the request body, with nothing stored and nothing fetched. Two things are worth copying. Routes are mounted at the root: plumber is a prefix-stripping framework here, so the platform forwards /summary rather than /apps/{slug}/summary, and a route that sends a Location back sends the bare path because the proxy re-adds the prefix on the way out. And a request body is server-side input: MAX_VALUES caps how many numbers one request may carry, because plumber, like Shiny, is one R process and a caller who posts a million values would otherwise decide how long the app is busy for.
items.author: Launchpad

env.name: API_TITLE
env.description: Heading on the index page and in /health.

env.name: MAX_VALUES
env.description: Most values one request may carry. Anything below 10 falls back to the default.

items.notes: The file is called plumber.R because that is the name plumber::plumb() finds with no argument, and it is what Launchpad detects — by a line scan for the #* annotations, never a parse, so a file that merely mentions plumber in a comment is not mistaken for an API. The generated Swagger UI at __docs__/ works, but the spec describes the routes as plumber sees them, at the root, while the browser is at /apps/{slug}/: read the shapes there and send real requests against the app's own URL.

items.name: Data Quality Report
items.summary: Point it at a CSV and it renders a page saying what is wrong with the file.
items.description: The R Markdown example. Seven checks — missing values, duplicate keys, categories that are the same thing spelled two ways, numbers outside Tukey's fences, and a histogram of every numeric column — over whatever REPORT_DATA names, with a seeded 1,209-row delivery export committed so there is a real report on screen before anybody points it at their own data. It is rendered once, at build time: Launchpad runs rmarkdown::render and serves the directory that falls out, so there is no R process behind the page and a re-render is a deploy, not a restart. Two sharp edges are stated rather than hidden. The render sees the app's environment variables and the output is published, so a document that prints a connection string has published it to everyone who can read the page. And a missing input file is a section, not a crash — on a fresh install the nightly export has not landed yet, and the report says so on its own front page instead of making somebody read a build log.
items.author: Launchpad

env.name: REPORT_TITLE
env.description: Document title.

env.name: REPORT_DATA
env.description: The CSV to profile, relative to the release directory.

env.name: REPORT_KEY
env.description: The column expected to be unique. Defaults to the first column.

env.name: REPORT_MAX_ROWS
env.description: Row cap on the read. The report says when it hit it.

items.notes: Launchpad decides which document is the app by counting the .Rmd files at the repository root, so there is exactly one here; two is ambiguous and the deploy refuses by name. That is also why the sample generator lives in data/ rather than beside the document — a root .R file is scanned for plumber annotations, so a helper script could otherwise decide the whole repository's framework. To refresh the numbers, deploy again, or give the app a render schedule, which is a full deploy on a cron expression.

items.name: Migration Console
items.summary: Request, approve and carry out moves of an app from one Launchpad install to another.
items.description: A change-request workflow for promotion between installs. A developer raises a request against one specific successful release of an app they own; a named reviewer reads it, looks at the attached documents and approves or rejects; the approved release is then pushed to the target install, straight away or at a scheduled time. The submitter never picks the destination — the first successful deploy binds a source app to a target app and every later request follows that link — and the approver chooses what the app is called there and who may see it, with the choice carrying to the next migration. Notes and documents live in two places: standing ones on the app, inherited by every request for it, and per-request ones for that release. The requester can name other people on a request, who can then read it, watch it and raise the next one. Everything is recorded per app, so "what has ever shipped from this app, and where is it now" is one page. Go, html/template and htmx, with its own Postgres database — no Node, no bundler, and no outbound request to anything but the installs you configure.
items.author: Launchpad

env.name: DATABASE_URL
env.description: A Postgres database for the console's own records — requests, approvals, documents and the ledger. Use one you already back up: this is an audit record of production deploys, not a cache. postgres://user:password@host:5432/dbname

env.name: TARGET_KEY_SECRET
env.description: Any long passphrase. Each target install's deploy key is encrypted with it before it is written to the database, so a database backup is not a copy of your estate's push credentials.

items.notes: Needs a Launchpad that can mint a read-scoped deploy key — 0.2.1 or later. Until then the Gallery shows it as needing a newer Launchpad rather than installing an app that cannot authenticate. The console holds a deploy key for each install it can push to, and each of those can deploy to any app on that install. Install it on the install your developers use, give it a read-scoped deploy key here and a deploy-scoped key on each target, and add a scheduled task pointing at /tasks/tick. The Install page inside the app lists every step and shows what is still outstanding.
